title: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Shipyards | Dye PT (US)
description: Liquid penetrant testing for US shipyards: stainless, aluminum and bronze welds, castings and repairs, mobilized to your yard. Request a PT quote.
h1: Liquid Penetrant Testing for Shipyards, Vessels and Ports
html:
Liquid penetrant testing (PT, also called dye penetrant inspection) finds surface-breaking cracks, laps, porosity and leaks paths in any non-porous material, which makes it the main surface method for the stainless, aluminum, bronze and copper-nickel parts that a ship is full of. Atlantis NDT sends technicians to US shipyards, repair yards and terminals for weld examination, casting checks and repair verification on those materials. To begin, request a PT inspection quote with the component list and material grades.

Where PT fits on a vessel

Hull steel is magnetic, and the first choice for its welds is magnetic particle inspection. Everything else on the ship needs a different tool. Piping systems for seawater cooling are copper-nickel or bronze. Chemical tankers and process vessels use stainless cargo tanks and piping. Superstructures, small craft, ferries and patrol boats are aluminum. Propellers and many valve bodies are cast bronze or nickel-aluminum bronze. Rudder bearing housings, sea chests and fittings are castings. None of these respond to a magnet, and PT works on all of them as long as the flaw is open to the surface.

The penetrant method is simple in principle: a low-surface-tension liquid is drawn into the crack by capillary action, the excess is removed, and a developer pulls the retained liquid back out so that a thin line becomes a visible indication. In practice, the quality depends on cleaning, dwell, removal technique and lighting, and on the person reading the result. For flaws below the surface or for remaining thickness, we use ultrasonic testing instead.

US rules and standards behind marine PT

US-flag commercial vessels are governed by Coast Guard rules in 46 CFR, with the classification society's rules and the contract specification setting the weld and material requirements. The method follows ASME Section V, Article 6, and the process standards ASTM E165 for the practice and ASTM E1417 for materials and process control. Navy work names NAVSEA T9074-AS-GIB-010/271 as the governing nondestructive testing document; we name it only as the document that controls that work and claim no NAVSEA qualification. Our technicians work under the company written practice to ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with a Level II performing and interpreting and an ASNT Level III approving procedures and reviewing reports.

As with every method, the acceptance criterion belongs to the specification, not to us. We classify and record indications; the owner, the yard quality manager or the surveyor decides on repair.

Stainless piping and cargo tank welds

Austenitic stainless is sensitive to contamination. ASTM E165 sets limits on the halogens and sulfur that penetrant materials may leave behind, because chlorides can start stress corrosion cracking in stainless steel, and sulfur can damage nickel alloys. For this reason, the penetrant, cleaner and developer are lot-certified for low halogen and sulfur, and the lot numbers go on the report. Wiping brushes and rags must not have touched carbon steel before, to avoid embedding iron in the surface. After examination, the developer and penetrant residue are removed so that nothing stays on the surface in service.

On a chemical tanker, the cargo tank welds, nozzle attachments and piping welds are all candidates for PT after fabrication or repair. Access is the real constraint: tank interiors are confined spaces with permits, ventilation and standby, and the vessel or yard controls those. Our penetrant testing of welds page covers the weld technique in more detail.

Aluminum, bronze and copper-nickel components

Aluminum welds crack at craters and along the centerline, and these cracks are fine and tight. A fluorescent penetrant under ultraviolet light shows them most clearly, which means the area needs to be darkened, so a tent or a shaded space is common on deck. Cast bronze propellers and nickel-aluminum bronze components have shrinkage, porosity and repair-weld cracks that PT reveals. Seawater piping in copper-nickel has welds and flanges that the owner may want checked after a repair. The penetrant selection depends on the surface: rougher cast or ground surfaces suit a water-washable system, while smooth machined surfaces suit a solvent-removable system that gives less background.

Where a casting or machined part is concerned, our penetrant testing of castings page describes the method for foundry and machine-shop work in any industry.

Technique details that decide results

  • Cleaning: remove paint, grease, rust and weld spatter from the area and a margin around it. Blasting or peening can smear metal over a crack, so an etch or a mechanical clean may be specified.
  • Temperature: ASME Section V Article 6 covers a standard surface temperature range from 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit. Outside it, the procedure must be qualified. A cold winter pier or a hot summer deck both fall outside.
  • Dwell time: the penetrant stays on the surface for the time set by the procedure, and must not dry out. The yard wind can dry it faster than expected.
  • Excess removal: a solvent-removable penetrant is wiped with a lightly dampened cloth and never flushed, which would wash it out of the crack.
  • Light: visible-dye examination needs enough white light at the surface; fluorescent examination needs low ambient light and a calibrated ultraviolet lamp.

Penetrant systems and how we choose one

ASTM E1417 sorts penetrant systems by type and method. Type I is fluorescent and Type II is visible dye; Methods A, B, C and D cover water-washable, lipophilic post-emulsifiable, solvent-removable and hydrophilic post-emulsifiable processes. Sensitivity levels run from low to ultra-high. A shipyard rarely needs the full range. Pier-side and deck work normally uses a visible-dye, solvent-removable kit, because it needs no water, power or darkening and is easy to carry up a ladder. Alloy fabrication shops and repair of critical bronze or aluminum parts more often use fluorescent systems for their sensitivity. The procedure names the system, and a comparison block with known cracks can be used to show the process is working on the day.

The choice also depends on what the owner will do next. If the surface is about to be painted, a solvent system that leaves little residue is easier to clean. If the surface is a seawater-wetted machined face, the owner may specify the cleanest possible removal. We state the planned system at quoting time, so the yard knows what materials, ventilation and ignition controls to expect.

Reading indications and judging them

An indication is not a defect until it has been evaluated. A bleed-out that is round suggests porosity or a pit; a continuous line suggests a crack or a cold lap; a scattered pattern at a weld toe may be undercut or rough profile. The technician waits for the developing time set by the procedure, looks at the surface under proper light, and measures each indication against the acceptance criterion. Borderline indications are wiped, re-developed and judged again. A relevant linear indication in a pressure-boundary or primary-structure weld is normally rejected; whether it is ground out, repaired or accepted by engineering waiver is the owner's decision.

Weld repair and drydock sequencing

A drydock period compresses the work of many trades into a short window, and PT sits between cleaning and painting. A weld repair on a stainless or aluminum item typically runs: grind out the defect, verify with PT that the crack is gone, weld, finish the surface and PT again. Each of those steps has to be accessible to us at the right moment. Penetrant chemicals are also a safety item on the site: the materials are flammable or combustible, and some products release vapor in a tank. The safety data sheets go to the yard for hot-work and confined-space reviews.

Rough hull weld caps, heavy paint and porous or scaled surfaces cause false indications. If a procedure requires it, the technician can ask for light grinding of the weld cap before the examination. Any indication that is not clearly relevant is re-examined after cleaning rather than called from a single look.

What the report contains

The PT report identifies the vessel or structure and each component by drawing, frame or tag number. It records the procedure and revision, specification and acceptance criterion, the penetrant system with type, method and sensitivity level, the manufacturer and lot numbers, the cleaning method, surface and ambient temperature, dwell and development time, and the light used. Each indication is recorded by location, shape and size, usually with a photograph, and marked accept or reject. The technician, qualification level and ASNT Level III reviewer are named. Areas that could not be examined are listed.

What to send for a quote

  • Component list or weld map, with materials and surface condition
  • The specification, class rule or NAVSEA requirement and the acceptance criterion
  • Whether the part is stainless or nickel alloy, so we can plan low-halogen materials
  • Location, access, confined-space and TWIC arrangements, and the drydock or repair sequence
  • Whether examination is before or after painting or final surface treatment

Where we work in the US marine market

Technicians travel to your site in these port and shipyard cities. Each page describes PT for the local market.

  • Norfolk: ship repair, piping and valve work on the Atlantic coast.
  • Pascagoula: Gulf Coast shipbuilding and alloy fabrication.
  • Mobile: aluminum vessels and offshore support craft.
  • San Diego: Pacific repair yards, with piping and casting repair.
  • Seattle: aluminum ferries and fishing vessels.
  • Tacoma: tug, barge and terminal steel and alloy work.
  • New Orleans: river and Gulf marine fabrication.
  • Baltimore: Chesapeake repair yards.

Training your own technicians

If your yard wants its own people on penetrant work, Atlantis offers PT Level 1 training and PT Level 2 training built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A, with the penetrant testing simulator for practice. The employer certifies under SNT-TC-1A. See maritime NDT training for marine programs, and the national penetrant testing page for the method in other industries.

What we do not do here

We do not perform radiography in the United States, and the specialist techniques are not offered on this page. PT cannot find flaws that do not reach the surface, and it fails on porous or heavily scaled surfaces. For class-credited thickness gauging, Atlantis is in the process of obtaining UR Z17 approval from DNV, Lloyd's Register and ABS; until a certificate is issued, readings are for the owner's own decisions, not for credit to a class survey. See maritime inspection for that scope.

faq.q: Is penetrant testing safe on stainless steel pipe?
faq.a: Yes, with the right materials. ASTM E165 limits halogens and sulfur in penetrant products used on stainless and nickel alloys, so we use lot-certified low-halogen products and record the lot numbers on the report.

faq.q: Can PT find cracks in aluminum ship structures?
faq.a: It finds surface-breaking cracks, pores and laps in aluminum welds, and fluorescent penetrant gives high sensitivity on fine cracks. The flaw must be open to the surface and the surface must be cleaned of oxide and contamination.

faq.q: What temperature range is allowed for penetrant testing?
faq.a: The standard range in ASME Section V Article 6 is roughly 40 to 125 degrees Fahrenheit at the surface. Outside it, the procedure has to be qualified, so we ask about the weather and surface conditions at quoting time.

faq.q: When is PT the wrong method on a ship?
faq.a: It is a poor choice on porous or heavily scaled surfaces, on subsurface flaws, and for thickness. On carbon steel welds magnetic particle inspection is usually faster and more sensitive, and UT covers the weld volume.

faq.q: Can you examine a propeller or bronze casting?
faq.a: Yes, on the surface. Cast bronze and nickel-aluminum bronze parts are routinely checked with PT for shrinkage, porosity and repair-weld cracks, and the acceptance limits come from the specification or class rule.

faq.q: What do you need from us to quote dye penetrant work?
faq.a: A component or weld list, material grades, the specification and acceptance criterion, surface condition, access and permit arrangements, TWIC needs, and where the work falls in the repair or drydock sequence.

faq.q: Can penetrant work be done inside tanks?
faq.a: Yes, with confined-space permits and ventilation controlled by the vessel or yard. The solvents are flammable, so the safety data sheets are reviewed with the yard before entry, and fluorescent work needs the space darkened.

faq.q: Is radiographic testing of ship piping part of the Atlantis offer?
faq.a: No. Atlantis does not perform radiography in the United States. For piping welds our surface examination is PT or MT, and for volume examination we offer ultrasonic testing where the code and owner accept it.
